covalent.note: Covalent radius; PubChem's values are those of Cordero et al., Dalton Trans. 2008, 2832. Value for l.s.; also 152(6)[h.s.].

vdw.note: Van der Waals radius (Los Alamos National Laboratory).

allen.note: Configuration energy (Allen electronegativity) in eV, not converted to the Pauling-like scale; Mann 2000b.

polarizability.note: Recommended value of the 2018 table: from experiment where it is precise enough, otherwise from high-level calculation.

crust.note: Jefferson Lab estimate for Earth's crust, via PubChem ('5.63×10⁴ milligrams per kilogram').

ocean.note: Jefferson Lab estimate for sea water, via PubChem ('2×10⁻³ milligrams per liter').

solar.note: Proto-solar (4.567 Ga ago) elemental mass fraction, column 'Elemental Mass Fractions' of ESM Table A13; the table gives no uncertainty (relative sigma of N(E) in Table 6 applies).

solarLogEps.note: A(E) = log10(N_E/N_H) + 12, 'Solar System Present' log (E/H)+12; basis: average of solar and meteoritic values; unc = 1 sigma in dex as printed.

body.note: In a 70 kg reference adult (ICRP Publication 23, 1975, Table 110).

crystal.reference: Zhang, J.; Guyot, F. (1999). Physics and Chemistry of Minerals 26, 206.
crystal.note: Measured at 298 K and 0 GPa, first point of a P–T series. Wyckoff's compilation (COD 9008536) gives 2.8665 Å at 298 K.

production.basis: mine production, iron ore, iron content

tonnesPerYear.note: World mine production, iron ore, iron content, 2025 (USGS: 1,600,000 thousand metric tons).

unitValue.note: Price, average unit value reported by mines, dollars per metric ton [Iron Ore], 2025; per kg of the material named, as USGS gives it.

molarHeatCapacity.note: At 25 °C and 1 bar, per mole of atoms, for the form stable at 25 °C (CRC Handbook, 95th ed.).

uses.text: Almost all iron ore (98 % in the U.S.) is made into steel.
Steel's largest market is construction (31 % of U.S. shipments), then service centres (26 %) and cars (15 %).
Foundries make cast iron, much of it from scrap; iron oxides colour concrete, paint, plastics and rubber.

allotropes.name: α-iron (ferrite)
allotropes.note: Body-centred cubic and magnetic: the form at room temperature.

allotropes.name: γ-iron (austenite)
allotropes.note: Face-centred cubic: the form at red to white heat, which can dissolve much more carbon.

allotropes.name: δ-iron
allotropes.note: Body-centred cubic again, just below the melting point.

hazards.note: Aggregated by PubChem from 6013 reports by companies to the ECHA C&L Inventory; the percentage after a statement is the share of reports that give it. 74.1 % of the reports (4458 of 6013) say iron does not meet the GHS hazard criteria.

crust.note: Earth's crust, as given (mg/kg is parts per million by mass).

ocean.note: Sea water, mg/L read as mg/kg: a litre of sea water is taken as one kilogram (it is slightly heavier; the difference cannot be seen on a logarithmic scale).

body.note: Grams in the 70 kg reference adult of ICRP Publication 23, divided by its mass.

origin.note: Read off Fig. 39 at the dotted 'age of the Sun' line (t = 9.2 Gyr after the Big Bang, 4.6 Gyr ago): pixel fractions of the stacked areas (agb 0.079, massive_stars 0.313, white_dwarfs 0.608); quantised to 0.05. Stack height 75 px. Cross-check with the paper's text: 'the fraction [of Fe from SNe Ia] is only 60% in our model, and the rest is mainly produced by HNe' (figure reading 0.608). Paper: 'For the elements from Ne to Ge, the newly synthesized amounts are very small for AGB stars, and the small green areas are mostly for mass loss.'

air.text: Keeps its shine in dry air, but rusts in moist air to hydrated iron oxides; fine iron powder can catch fire by itself.

water.text: Bulk iron does not react with pure water; in water containing air it rusts, and iron powder can release hydrogen.

acids.text: Dissolves readily in dilute mineral acids, giving hydrogen; cold concentrated nitric or sulfuric acid leave it untouched, hot ones attack it.

compounds.name: iron(III) oxide
compounds.note: haematite, the main iron ore; rust is its hydrated form

plantRole.text: Carries electrons in cytochromes and iron–sulfur proteins of photosynthesis and respiration, and is needed to make chlorophyll; shortage yellows young leaves between the veins.

humanRole.text: Binds oxygen in haemoglobin and myoglobin and carries electrons in respiration.

roles.text: Carries oxygen in haemoglobin and myoglobin; piglets reared indoors are born with small reserves and become anaemic without extra iron.
Some invertebrates, such as sipunculid worms, bind oxygen with haemerythrin, which holds it between two iron atoms.
Iron proteins, with haem, iron–sulfur clusters or other iron centres, make up about 2 % of yeast proteins, many of them in respiration.
Built into iron–sulfur clusters, ancient cofactors found throughout life that carry electrons, bind substrates and help control genes.
A rare exception: the Lyme disease bacterium Borrelia burgdorferi appears to do without iron, using manganese in its place.
Built into iron–sulfur clusters, ancient cofactors found throughout life that carry electrons, bind substrates and help control genes.
An extreme case: about 86 % of the proteins of the acid-loving Ferroplasma acidiphilum bind iron.

history.nameOrigin: From the Old English iren (isern), a word of Germanic origin.
history.symbolNote: Fe comes from the Latin ferrum.

prose.text: Iron is the most used of all metals, mostly as steel, and the main ingredient of Earth's core; in our blood it carries oxygen inside haemoglobin, and plants need it to make chlorophyll, so iron-starved leaves turn pale. Its common isotope, iron-56, about 91.8 % of natural iron, has one of the most tightly bound nuclei of all, which is why the fusion fires of massive stars stop releasing energy once their cores turn to iron. The atom, [Ar] 3d⁶ 4s² (ground term ⁵D₄), has four unpaired d electrons, and in the solid metal the spins of neighbouring atoms line up, making iron magnetic.
